entry.title: Testing Malus’s law with Arduino
entry.content:
• physics
  • optics
  • electronics
  • arduino
  • experimental-science
  • lego
  • ldr
  • resistor
  • adafruit

In my fifth year of high school, I investigated Malus’s law: how the intensity of polarized light changes as we rotate a polarizing filter. I built an apparatus using LEGO, a laser diode, two polarizers, a photoresistor, and an Arduino Uno. The experiment brought together the physics of light and the electronics needed to measure it.

The most interesting part came when the first results did not follow the curve I expected. I had to look beyond the optical setup and question how I was converting the sensor readings into light intensity. Here, I’ll walk through the experiment, the original measurements, and the limits of the interpretation I used at the time.

Information:

You can download all 65 readings as a CSV, with column definitions and calculation notes. The interactive charts below use my experimental data. Hover or tap a point for its voltage and resistance, drag to zoom, and click a legend entry to hide or show a series. Double-click the plot to reset its view; a static chart is available below each plot.

1. What we expect from two polarizers

A linearly polarized light wave has an electric field that oscillates along a fixed direction perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

An ideal linear polarizer transmits the electric-field component parallel to its transmission axis. If the incident field has amplitude \(E_0\) and makes an angle \(\theta\) with that axis, the transmitted amplitude is

\[E = E_0\cos\theta.\]

Because intensity is proportional to the square of the field amplitude, we obtain Malus’s law:

\[I(\theta)=I_0\cos^2\theta.\]

Here, \(I_0\) is the intensity of the linearly polarized beam immediately before the analyzer, which is the second polarizer in my apparatus. The angle \(\theta\) is measured between the transmission axes of the two filters. For the ideal case, parallel axes transmit the maximum, crossed axes transmit no light, and a 45° angle gives half the maximum. This is the projection argument described in OpenStax’s explanation of polarization.

Relative angle Ideal transmitted fraction
0° 100%
30° 75%
45° 50%
60° 25%
90° 0%
180° 100%

I suggest keeping the distinction between field amplitude and intensity in mind: the projection gives a cosine, while the intensity follows its square. The pattern repeats every 180°, since reversing a filter’s axis gives the same transmission direction.

2. Building the apparatus

My optical path was straightforward:

Laser → fixed polarizer → rotating analyzer → photoresistor.

The first polarizer established a fixed polarization direction, while the second let me vary the angle without rotating the laser itself. The laser pointed downward through the filters toward the sensor. I used a white LEGO support to hold the components and allow manual adjustment of their alignment. The presentation also describes an opaque cardboard enclosure around the structure to reduce interference from room light. The detector was an LDR, or light-dependent resistor: its resistance decreases as more light reaches it. The Arduino measured the voltage across it in a voltage divider, then sent the readings over USB serial. My report describes averaging multiple readings for each measurement and switching the laser on only during acquisition to limit heating. The exact number of samples and acquisition timing are not recorded in the supplied report, so I cannot reconstruct those details here. For each main measurement set, I recorded 13 angles in 15° steps, covering a half-turn. The report assigns an angular uncertainty of approximately ±2°, based on the markings and manual positioning of the filters.

3. From Arduino voltage to resistance

The circuit used a nominal 5 V supply and a 100 kΩ fixed resistor in series with the LDR. The fixed-resistor value appears in both the presentation’s circuit diagram and the spreadsheet formulas. The voltage was measured across the LDR, rather than across the fixed resistor.

Calling the measured voltage \(V\), the supply \(V_s\), and the fixed resistance \(R_f\), the divider gives

\[V=V_s\frac{R_{\mathrm{LDR}}}{R_f+R_{\mathrm{LDR}}}.\]

Solving for the sensor resistance gives

\[R_{\mathrm{LDR}}=R_f\frac{V}{V_s-V}.\]

For example, the first set’s reading at 0° was 0.4494 V. Using the nominal circuit values, we obtain

\[R_{\mathrm{LDR}}=100\,\mathrm{k\Omega}\times\frac{0.4494}{5-0.4494} \approx9.8756\,\mathrm{k\Omega}.\]

The direction of the response can seem surprising at first: more light lowers the LDR resistance, which also lowers the voltage measured across it. We therefore cannot treat the voltage itself as a quantity proportional to light intensity.

4. Checking the laser before testing the law

Before interpreting the two-filter measurements, I rotated a single filter relative to the stationary laser and support. The detected signal changed with orientation. In my original report, I interpreted this as evidence that the laser beam was partially polarized.

This chart uses normalized inverse resistance as a sensor proxy, rather than a calibrated intensity measurement. Its vertical axis starts at 75% to make the variation visible. The control suggested that I should not assume the incident beam was unpolarized, although it did not independently determine its degree of polarization. Alignment changes could also affect such a measurement.

Keeping the first polarizer fixed gave the main experiment a defined input polarization while I rotated only the analyzer. The familiar statement that a polarizer transmits half the incident intensity applies to ideal, unpolarized incident light; it should not be assumed for this laser. For the angular comparison, I instead worked with relative signals.

5. The first conversion did not reproduce the expected curve

My initial analysis assumed a simple inverse relationship between resistance and light level \(L\):

\[R=\frac{k}{L}.\]

If that model were adequate, an unknown constant \(k\) would cancel when taking a ratio:

\[\frac{L}{L_{\mathrm{ref}}}=\frac{R_{\mathrm{ref}}}{R}.\]

The report initially used a reference measurement with only the fixed polarizer in place. For Set 1, that reference was 0.4492 V, corresponding to approximately 9.8708 kΩ. The workbook also normalized each two-filter sweep to its own inferred maximum, using the minimum resistance in that sweep. I use this second convention consistently in the comparison charts:

\[y_{\mathrm{inverse}}=\frac{R_{\min}}{R}.\]

This normalization makes the maximum equal to one, but it does not establish an absolute light calibration or measure the analyzer’s insertion loss. The first sweep shows why that distinction matters.

Angle Measured voltage (V) Derived resistance (kΩ) Inverse-model ratio Ideal \(\cos^2\theta\)
−45° 0.4950 10.9878 0.8988 0.5000
0° 0.4494 9.8756 1.0000 1.0000
30° 0.5097 11.3511 0.8700 0.7500
45° 0.5535 12.4480 0.7934 0.5000
60° 0.6676 15.4095 0.6409 0.2500
90° 4.0088 404.4391 0.0244 0.0000

At 45°, this conversion suggests roughly 79% of the maximum, whereas the ideal prediction is 50%. The differences are too large to describe as a close quantitative match. The readings at −45° and +45° also differ, even though the ideal curve is symmetric. A sensor conversion alone cannot explain every feature of the data.

6. Trying a different sensor model

I then explored an empirical exponential conversion:

\[L=\alpha e^{-\beta R}.\]

Normalizing to the same sweep’s maximum removes \(\alpha\):

\[y_{\mathrm{exponential}}=\frac{L}{L_{\max}} =e^{\beta(R_{\min}-R)}.\]

The workbook uses \(\beta=0.47\,\mathrm{k\Omega}^{-1}\) for Sets 1, 2, and 3. When resistance is expressed in ohms, the equivalent value is \(4.7\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{\Omega}^{-1}\). The units must match so that the exponent is dimensionless.

The red points use the original inverse model, while the green points use the exponential model. The blue line is the ideal prediction, and the horizontal bars show the report’s ±2° angular uncertainty. Both sets of points come from the same measured voltages. The curve changes because the conversion changes, rather than because I collected a new set of readings.

The exponential model brings many points closer to the expected shape, but substantial discrepancies remain. For example, the converted values at −45° and +45° are approximately 0.593 and 0.298, compared with a theoretical value of 0.5 for both. I would describe this as improved agreement under an empirical model, rather than a precise verification of the law.

An LDR is not automatically a calibrated light meter. Its response depends on the particular sensor and the illumination conditions, as discussed in Adafruit’s photocell guide. The exponential expression here was an exploratory approximation from my original project, not a universal law for photoresistors.

7. Repeated measurements and Set 4

The workbook contains two further sweeps analyzed with the same value of \(\beta\). They cover 0° to 180°, rather than the −90° to +90° interval used in Set 1.

A fourth measurement set records a run made under different conditions. It uses \(\beta=0.07\,\mathrm{k\Omega}^{-1}\), rather than 0.47. The spreadsheet notes better shielding from ambient light and warmer, more humid conditions as possible reasons for differences between runs; these were proposed explanations, rather than separately measured causes. It also flags possible positioning errors in the first and last readings.

For this chart, I shifted Set 4’s recorded angles from 90°–270° to −90°–90° by subtracting 180°. This leaves the theoretical cosine-squared values unchanged. I kept all 13 measurements, including the two flagged endpoints.

To compare the curves numerically for this article, I recalculated the root-mean-square deviation from the ideal prediction:

\[\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left(y_i-\cos^2\theta_i\right)^2}.\]

Each row below uses all 13 points, with equal weight and the workbook’s original \(\beta\) value. These are descriptive deviations in normalized units, not uncertainty estimates or formal goodness-of-fit tests.

Measurement set Inverse-model RMSE Exponential-model RMSE \(\beta\) (kΩ⁻¹)
Set 1 0.278 0.116 0.47
Set 2 0.266 0.058 0.47
Set 3 0.205 0.070 0.47
Set 4 0.058 0.056 0.07

The exponential conversion reduces the deviation in the first three sets, while Set 4 shows only a small difference between the two conversions. The change in \(\beta\) is also a reason to avoid treating it as a transferable sensor calibration.

8. What the experiment could establish

The experiment showed a repeatable dependence of the detected signal on the relative orientation of the polarizers. Its broad pattern is consistent with the expected transmission maximum for aligned filters and minimum for crossed filters. It also exposed how strongly an inferred intensity curve can depend on the detector model.

There is an important limit to the calibration argument: I selected an empirical conversion because it made the data resemble the law I wanted to test. That agreement cannot independently validate both Malus’s law and the sensor conversion. An independent calibration would be needed to separate those questions.

The source material does not provide repeated-reading scatter, a complete voltage uncertainty budget, or an independently measured light-to-resistance calibration. For that reason, I have not added vertical error bars or claimed agreement within experimental uncertainty. The recorded decimal places describe the stored readings, rather than establishing their accuracy.

The divider also becomes sensitive to voltage error as its reading approaches the supply:

\[\frac{dR}{dV}=R_f\frac{V_s}{(V_s-V)^2}.\]

That matters near crossed polarizers, where a high LDR resistance pushes the measured voltage toward 5 V. Background light, imperfect extinction, alignment, sensor response time, and heating are further effects I would investigate before assigning a discrepancy to the optical law.

If I repeated the project, I would first calibrate the detector independently, record dark readings, repeat each angle, and measure the supply voltage. I would also compare the result with a photodiode operated in a characterized linear regime. Those changes would make the comparison less dependent on choosing a convenient conversion afterward.

Experimental data

I have provided a CSV containing all 65 readings and the derived quantities used here, with column definitions and calculation notes. It includes the laser control and Sets 1–4. The CSV and charts are a new extraction of the original workbook; the RMSE comparison is an additional calculation for this article.

Looking back, the most useful lesson was learning to question the measurement chain. The Arduino supplied voltages, the circuit let me derive resistances, and only a further model turned those resistances into relative light levels. Understanding each of those steps was as much a part of the experiment as rotating the polarizers.
entry.summary: An experiment with polarized light, a LEGO apparatus, and an Arduino light sensor-and what I learned when the measurements did not match the expected curve.

entry.title: Building a small MVC library in PHP

link.title: Building a small MVC library in PHP

entry.content:
Information:

The repo with the following code is avaible on GitHub.

A PHP application can begin with a single page. As soon as we add another page, a form, and a shared header, that simple file starts doing several jobs at once. Building a small library gives each job a home and makes the next page easier to write.

Let’s build toward Simple MVC using PHP 8.3 or newer. We’ll start with a response, introduce one feature at a time, and finish with automated tests and releases. You only need basic PHP: variables, arrays, functions, and a little HTML. Classes and other unfamiliar syntax will be explained as they appear.

The early code examples are small building blocks, not complete replacements for the library files. Each section explains what to add or change. The final application example uses the finished library’s API.

1. Give every request one starting point

Our first page needs very little:

<?php
// demo/index.php
header('Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8');
echo 'Hello, world!';

header() tells the browser what kind of response it is receiving. echo writes its body. Headers must be sent before output, so the file begins with <?php, without a blank line before it.

We could create a separate PHP file for every page. Instead, we’ll keep index.php as the entry point and let it choose what to run. This pattern is called a front controller: every application request enters through the same door.

For local development, PHP has a built-in server. From the project directory, run:

php -S localhost:8000 -t demo demo/index.php

Here, demo is the public document directory, and demo/index.php is the development router script. Visit http://localhost:8000/. The built-in server is for development; a production server needs its own front-controller configuration.

2. Let Composer find our classes

As we move code into separate files, manually writing require for every class becomes repetitive. Composer can load classes when PHP first uses them.

We give the library this directory structure:

project/
  composer.json
  src/
    Controllers/
    Controllers/Attributes/
    Http/
    Routers/
    Users/
    Utils/
  demo/
    index.php
    Views/
      Home/
      Shared/

The relevant part of composer.json is:

{
  "name": "richie314/simple-mvc",
  "require": {
    "php": ">=8.3"
  },
  "autoload": {
    "psr-4": {
      "Richie314\\SimpleMvc\\": "src/"
    }
  },
  "autoload-dev": {
    "psr-4": {
      "Richie314\\SimpleMvc\\Demo\\": "demo/"
    }
  }
}

A namespace gives a class a full name, avoiding clashes with similarly named classes in other packages. The PSR-4 mapping says that Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Controller belongs in src/Controllers/Controller.php. The double backslashes above are how JSON represents a literal backslash.

Run composer install, then add this to the entry point:

require dirname(__DIR__) . '/vendor/autoload.php';

__DIR__ is the directory containing the current PHP file. Since index.php lives in demo, dirname(__DIR__) takes us to the project root.

The development mapping loads our example classes from a checkout. Applications installing the package through Composer configure their own application-class autoloading.

3. Give HTTP values readable names

A successful page usually has status 200. A missing page uses 404. Numbers work, but names communicate intent more clearly.

Add an enum in src/Http/StatusCode.php:

<?php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Http;

enum StatusCode: int
{
    case Ok = 200;
    case Created = 201;
    case SeeOther = 303;
    case BadRequest = 400;
    case NotAuthorized = 401;
    case NotFound = 404;
    case ServerError = 500;
}

An enum is a defined set of named values. This is a shortened selection of the finished library’s cases. StatusCode::Ok is an enum value; StatusCode::Ok->value is the integer 200 needed by PHP’s HTTP functions.

Add the same idea for request methods:

<?php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Http;

enum Method: string
{
    case Get = 'GET';
    case Post = 'POST';
    case Put = 'PUT';
    case Patch = 'PATCH';
    case Delete = 'DELETE';
    case Head = 'HEAD';
    case Options = 'OPTIONS';
    case Trace = 'TRACE';
}

GET commonly retrieves a page. POST commonly submits a form. We can convert the server’s request method into the enum with:

$method = Method::from(strtoupper($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']));

from() rejects values outside the enum. Having a method case does not yet give us body parsing or routing rules for that method; those are separate decisions.

4. Move response-writing into a base controller

Our entry point should choose a page rather than build every response itself. Introduce a controller, a class whose public methods handle requests. We’ll call those methods actions.

A shared base class can provide the response-writing code:

<?php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers;

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Http\StatusCode;

class Controller
{
    protected function Content(
        string $type,
        string $content,
        StatusCode|int $statusCode = StatusCode::Ok,
    ): StatusCode {
        if (!$statusCode instanceof StatusCode) {
            $statusCode = StatusCode::from($statusCode);
        }

        http_response_code($statusCode->value);
        header("Content-Type: $type");
        header('Content-Length: ' . strlen($content));
        echo $content;

        return $statusCode;
    }
}

protected means the helper is available inside this class and its child classes. It is not intended to become a public action. The StatusCode|int type accepts either an enum case or an integer, while the return type promises an enum.

An application controller can now extend the base class:

<?php
// demo/HomeController.php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Demo;

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Controller;
use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Http\StatusCode;

class HomeController extends Controller
{
    public function index(): StatusCode
    {
        return $this->Content('text/plain; charset=UTF-8', 'Hello, world!');
    }
}

extends makes the shared helpers available through $this, the current object. return passes the helper’s result back to whoever called the action.

The response has two effects: it sends content to the browser and returns a status for our PHP code to inspect. Merely returning an enum does not send an HTTP status; the response helper does that work.

5. Map URLs to actions

We now need to turn a path such as /hello into a controller and method. Add a Router class in src/Routers/Router.php.

Its first job is to store a route table:

private array $routes = [];

public function AddRouteAction(
    string $route,
    string $controller,
    string $action,
): void {
    $this->routes[$route] = [
        'controller' => $controller,
        'action' => $action,
    ];
}

A route is just a lookup entry. This registration says, “For /hello, create HomeController and run index”:

$router->AddRouteAction('/hello', HomeController::class, 'index');

::class returns the full class name as a string. It does not create an object.

Next, add dispatching. The important operations are:

$path = parse_url($uri, PHP_URL_PATH);
$route = $this->routes[$path];
$controllerClass = $route['controller'];
$action = $route['action'];

$controller = new $controllerClass(
    requestPath: $uri,
    requestMethod: $this->RequestMethod,
);

return $controller->$action();

This fragment assumes the router has read the request method, the base controller has gained matching constructor parameters, and the route exists. We’ll add missing-route handling shortly.

The syntax requestPath: $uri is a named argument. PHP matches the value to a parameter by name instead of position.

The path and query string are different parts of the URL: /hello?name=Ada has path /hello. Extracting the path lets the same route handle different query values. Routes match exactly; /hello and /hello/ remain different routes.

6. Pass query parameters to actions

A fixed greeting is a useful start. A personalized greeting is more interesting. Change the action to accept a parameter:

public function index(string $first_name = 'World'): StatusCode
{
    return $this->Content(
        'text/plain; charset=UTF-8',
        'Hello, ' . $first_name . '!',
    );
}

The default value means a visitor can omit the name. In the router, parse the query and normalize field names:

$query = parse_url($uri, PHP_URL_QUERY);
$parameters = [];

if (is_string($query) && $query !== '') {
    parse_str($query, $parameters);
}

$named = [];
foreach ($parameters as $name => $value) {
    $named[str_replace('-', '_', $name)] = $value;
}

Replace the direct method call with:

return call_user_func_array([$controller, $action], $named);

With string array keys, PHP passes these as named arguments. /hello?first-name=Ada becomes $first_name = 'Ada' in the action.

This convenience makes parameter names part of the action’s interface. Extra fields, missing required arguments, or array values where strings are expected can cause invocation errors. Type declarations help describe inputs, but application code still needs to validate what those inputs mean.

7. Add form submissions

A browser form normally sends its fields through POST:

<form method="post" action="/hello">
  <label>Name <input name="first-name" required></label>
  <button type="submit">Say hello</button>
</form>

Extend the router’s parameter parser so it selects the input source first:

switch ($this->RequestMethod) {
    case Method::Get:
        // Parse the query string as in the previous section.
        break;
    case Method::Post:
        $parameters = $_POST;
        break;
}

Then apply the same hyphen-to-underscore conversion. Both request types can call the same action without copying the binding code.

Before using a submitted name, the action can trim it and reject an empty result:

$first_name = trim($first_name);
if ($first_name === '') {
    return $this->BadRequest('Please enter a name.');
}

We’ll add the BadRequest() helper in the error-handling step. The HTML required attribute helps the browser’s user, but the server still checks the input because requests can arrive without that browser validation.

The library does not automatically decode JSON request bodies or bind parameters for other methods. Route registration also does not restrict which HTTP method may call an action. An action that changes data should check $this->RequestMethod and apply the application’s authentication and CSRF protection rules.

8. Move HTML into a view

A controller becomes hard to read if it contains a large HTML string. Move the markup to demo/Views/Home/index.php:

<h1>Hello, <?= htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') ?>!</h1>

A view is a template responsible for presentation. <?= ... ?> is the short form of <?php echo ...; ?>.

Notice the escaping. If someone enters <strong>Ada</strong>, we want to display those characters as a name, rather than let them inject markup. htmlspecialchars() performs HTML escaping at the point of output.

Change the action to describe what to render:

public function index(string $name = 'World'): StatusCode
{
    return $this->Render('Home/index', ['name' => $name], 'Welcome');
}

Add view lookup to the base controller. It combines a trusted application directory with Views/ and the view name. For a name without a dot, the finished library tries .php, .html, and .htm, then tries the shared-view directory.

The first rendering idea is simply:

$view_file = $this->ViewFileName($view);
extract($data, EXTR_SKIP);
require $view_file;

extract() turns ['name' => 'Ada'] into a local $name variable. EXTR_SKIP prevents those values from overwriting existing local variables. We pass an explicitly constructed data array, never an entire request array, and the view name comes from application code rather than visitor input.

This fragment shows the core operation. A usable Render() also checks for a missing file, sends a status, and returns that status.

9. Add a shared layout without losing view variables

The next page needs the same document structure and header. Instead of copying them, introduce demo/Views/Shared/Layout.php:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title><?= htmlspecialchars($title, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') ?></title>
</head>
<body>
  <header>A tiny PHP application</header>
  <main><?php $RenderBody(); ?></main>
</body>
</html>

$RenderBody is a function stored in a variable. The layout chooses where to call it, and that call includes the page’s view.

Update the rendering code to prepare variables for both places:

$view_variables = array_merge($data, $this->ViewBag, [
    'title' => $title,
    'status_code' => $statusCode->value,
    'user' => $this->User,
    'P' => $this->PathPrefix,
]);

$view_variables['RenderBody'] = function () use ($view_file, $view_variables): void {
    extract($view_variables, EXTR_SKIP);
    require $view_file;
};

extract($view_variables, EXTR_SKIP);
require $layout_file_path;

A function has its own variable scope. The use (...) clause explicitly brings the selected file and data into this closure, a function created inside another piece of code. Without extracting inside the closure, the body would not receive $name, even though the layout could receive it.

array_merge() gives later string keys priority. The order above means default view variables override action data, and built-in variables such as $title override both. Internal renderer variable names are reserved.

Use require for templates, not require_once: each render should produce its output, even if the same layout was already rendered earlier in the request.

To share a site name across controllers, add a router method that stores defaults and passes them into each controller’s constructor:

$router->SetDefaultVariable('siteName', 'My application');

The controller stores these in $this->ViewBag. The layout can then escape and display $siteName just like any other view variable.

10. Give application data a separate home

We now have a controller and a view. Where does the model fit?

The model is the application’s data and the rules around that data. It does not have to be a database table or extend a framework class. Start with a tiny greeting rule in demo/Greeting.php:

<?php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Demo;

class Greeting
{
    public static function ForName(string $name): string
    {
        $name = trim($name);
        return 'Hello, ' . ($name === '' ? 'World' : $name) . '!';
    }
}

static lets us call this method on the class itself. Edit the controller action:

public function index(string $name = 'World'): StatusCode
{
    return $this->Render(
        'Home/index',
        ['message' => Greeting::ForName($name)],
        'Welcome',
    );
}

Replace the view’s heading to match the new data key:

<h1><?= htmlspecialchars($message, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') ?></h1>

The model builds the message, the controller coordinates the request, and the view renders HTML. The model does not escape HTML because another caller might want the same message as plain text or JSON.

Later, models may read a database. The library can share an optional mysqli connection through Router::SetDbConnection(), making it available as $this->DB in controllers. Actual queries and application rules remain the application’s responsibility. No database is required for the greeting example.

11. Register a whole controller

After adding several actions, repeated registrations become tedious. Add AddController() to discover public methods and register each beneath a base path:

$router->AddController(HomeController::class, '/');

The implementation inspects public method names, skips names beginning with _ or #, and maps the base path to index().

The mapping becomes:

URL Action
/ HomeController::index()
/index HomeController::index()
/hello HomeController::hello() if that public method exists

Keep internal helpers protected or private. If an application needs to expose only selected actions, explicit AddRouteAction() registrations remain the clearer choice. Existing routes still work; the convenience method only saves repetitive setup.

12. Support installation beneath a URL prefix

The application may live at https://example.com/myapp/ rather than the domain root. Add a prefix to the router:

$router = new Router(
    pathPrefix: '/myapp',
    applicationInstallationPath: __DIR__,
);

The prefix is a URL path. The installation path is a filesystem directory. They solve different problems and should not be confused.

Change route registration to prepend the prefix:

$this->routes[$this->PathPrefix . $route] = [
    'controller' => $controller,
    'action' => $action,
];

Keep registering routes such as /hello, not /myapp/hello. The router now supplies the prefix. In views, $P provides that same value for links:

<a href="<?= htmlspecialchars($P, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') ?>/hello">Hello</a>

An empty prefix keeps root installations working. Avoid an extra trailing slash in a configured prefix, because concatenation is literal.

13. Return useful error responses

A visitor will eventually request a missing page. Check the route table before accessing it. Select ErrorController::NotFoundHandler() when the path is absent, and clear the action arguments for that fallback.

Why clear them? /missing?unexpected=value should remain a 404. Passing unexpected into a zero-argument error handler would create another error.

Add helpers to the base controller for NotFound(), BadRequest(), NotAuthorized(), and InternalError(). Each sets the corresponding status and uses Views/Shared/Error.php when present. A missing error view should produce plain text with the intended status, not another missing-view error.

A small error view could be:

<h1>We could not complete that request</h1>
<p><?= htmlspecialchars($main_banner, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') ?></p>

Finally, put controller construction, action filters, and action invocation inside the router’s try block:

try {
    // Create the controller, run its attributes, and call the action.
} catch (\Throwable $ex) {
    if (headers_sent()) {
        throw $ex;
    }

    // Create ErrorController and return InternalErrorHandler($ex).
}

Throwable covers exceptions and PHP errors. Before output starts, the router can send a server-error response. After headers have been sent, it cannot reliably replace the response, so it rethrows the problem.

The current error helper uses an exception’s message as its banner. Applications serving public traffic should arrange error handling so private exception details are logged rather than displayed to visitors.

14. Add JSON responses

An action may serve JavaScript or another application instead of an HTML page. Add a Json() helper that encodes a value and delegates to Content():

public function hello(string $name = 'World'): StatusCode
{
    return $this->Json(['message' => Greeting::ForName($name)]);
}

The essential encoding call is:

$content = json_encode($object, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
return $this->Content('application/json', $content, $statusCode);

JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR turns an encoding failure into a JsonException, which the router can handle. We avoid silently returning an empty or misleading response.

To allow extra JSON flags, add a separate helper:

return $this->JsonWithOptions(
    ['url' => '/hello'],
    flags: JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES,
);

Keeping Json()’s signature unchanged matters for existing applications that override it in a child controller. Adding an optional argument to a parent method can still make an older override incompatible. A new helper provides the extra behavior without changing that contract.

15. Redirect after a successful form submission

After a form saves data, sending the browser to a different page avoids displaying the result of the submission directly. Add an explicit-status redirect helper:

return $this->RedirectWithStatus('/saved', StatusCode::SeeOther);

The core implementation is:

header("Location: $url", response_code: $statusCode->value);
return $statusCode;

A 303 See Other tells the browser to follow the destination using GET. The application must also register the destination route.

A response helper does not automatically stop PHP. Returning it from the action ensures the action ends at that point. Do not take the destination directly from untrusted input without checking it.

The existing Redirect() API is preserved: it returns the 301 enum even though PHP normally sends 302 for its bare Location header. New code can use RedirectWithStatus() when the returned value and actual response must agree.

16. Run a login check before an action

Repeating a login check inside every protected action is easy to forget. Introduce a small interface for code that runs before an action:

<?php
namespace Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Attributes;

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Controller;

interface Attribute
{
    public function DoWork(
        Controller $controller,
        string $action,
        array $parameters,
    ): void;
}

An interface describes what a class must provide. Here, a filter must implement DoWork().

The built-in RequireLogin class implements that interface and is marked with PHP’s #[\Attribute]. That marker permits using it as metadata above an action:

#[\Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Attributes\RequireLogin(loginPath: '/login')]
public function account(): StatusCode
{
    return $this->Json(['name' => $this->User->Name]);
}

In the router, use reflection to discover and run those objects before invoking the action:

$attributes = (new \ReflectionMethod($controllerClass, $action))
    ->getAttributes(
        \Richie314\SimpleMvc\Controllers\Attributes\Attribute::class,
        \ReflectionAttribute::IS_INSTANCEOF,
    );

foreach ($attributes as $attribute) {
    $attribute->newInstance()->DoWork($controller, $action, $named);
}

Reflection lets PHP inspect a class or method while the program is running. The filter interface prevents the router from treating unrelated metadata as an action filter.

The application loads an authenticated User and passes it to $router->SetUser($user). RequireLogin checks whether that user exists. If absent, it records the requested URI in a cookie, redirects to login, and terminates the request. With requireAdmin: true, it additionally checks the user’s Admin flag.

The attribute enforces access; it does not implement account registration, sessions, or password persistence. The application supplies those pieces and a login action. Only call SetUser() with identity information established by the application’s authentication process.

17. Add cookie options without changing existing calls

The login redirect introduces a browser cookie. A helper keeps the expiration calculation in one place:

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Utils\Cookie;

Cookie::Set('preference', 'compact', 3600);

3600 is a lifetime in seconds, not an absolute timestamp. Internally, the helper adds it to time().

For configurable security attributes, add SetWithOptions():

Cookie::SetWithOptions(
    'preference',
    'compact',
    3600,
    path: '/myapp',
    secure: true,
    sameSite: 'Lax',
);

secure restricts transmission to HTTPS. HTTP-only cookies are the default, preventing browser scripts from reading them. SameSite influences when a browser includes the cookie in requests coming from another site; it is not a replacement for an application’s CSRF protection.

Keep the original method and defaults intact. As with JSON options, the separate method also preserves existing subclass signatures.

Cookie reads come from the incoming request:

$value = Cookie::Get('preference'); // null when absent
Cookie::DeleteWithOptions('preference', path: '/myapp');

Writing a response cookie does not rewrite $_COOKIE. Deletion sends an expired cookie and must match the original path and domain. Cookies, like other headers, must be written before output.

18. Add a password helper

Passwords should be verified against stored hashes, not stored as readable text. Wrap PHP’s password functions:

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Utils\Security;

$hash = Security::Hash('a long example password');
$matches = Security::TestPassword('a long example password', $hash);

The library uses password_hash() with bcrypt and password_verify(). Verification does not require decrypting anything. The stored hash contains the information PHP needs for comparison.

The helper marks plaintext password parameters with #[\SensitiveParameter], which redacts their values from stack traces. This does not stop application code from logging a password directly, so keep it out of logs.

For compatibility, hashing an empty string returns an empty string, and verification with an empty password or hash returns false. Application validation should reject empty passwords before storage. Password-length and storage policies belong to the application too.

19. Read configuration from environment-backed files

A deployment may provide a setting directly or place it in a secret file. Add a helper with a predictable precedence:

$password = Security::LoadEnvironmentOrFromFile('DB_PASSWORD', 'fallback');

It first checks $_ENV['DB_PASSWORD']. If absent, it looks for a filename in $_ENV['DB_PASSWORD_FILE'] and reads that file. If neither provides a value, it returns the fallback.

The important condition is:

$content = file_get_contents($filename);
if ($content === false) {
    return $default;
}
return $content;

Use === false, not if (!$content). An empty file and a file containing 0 are both readable files with valid contents. A strict comparison distinguishes those values from a failed read.

The helper uses $_ENV, not getenv(), and preserves file contents, including trailing newlines. The application’s environment setup needs to populate the expected keys.

20. Serve a file and normalize uploads

A download action should not duplicate MIME detection and attachment headers. The controller’s file helper can supply them:

public function download(): StatusCode
{
    return $this->File(__DIR__ . '/Private/report.pdf');
}

The application must create that file and apply any required access checks. Use a trusted path; do not append arbitrary visitor input to a private directory path.

File() checks for a missing path, detects its MIME type, optionally adds attachment headers, and sends the content. It loads the whole file into memory, so it is suitable for modest downloads rather than a general large-file streaming solution.

For uploads, the utility class normalizes PHP’s different single-file and multiple-file structures:

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Utils\File;

foreach (File::UploadingFiles('attachments') as $upload) {
    if ($upload['error'] !== UPLOAD_ERR_OK) {
        continue;
    }
    // Apply the application's size/type rules, then move_uploaded_file().
}

The matching form needs enctype="multipart/form-data" and a field such as <input type="file" name="attachments[]" multiple>.

Normalization makes iteration easier. It does not validate a file or make its original name trustworthy. The application chooses safe storage names and validates the content before accepting it.

21. Document the public contract

At this point, method names alone do not explain enough. Add PHPDoc above functions so editors can show meaningful help:

/**
 * Set or replace a default variable for controller views.
 *
 * @param string $key Variable name; an empty name is ignored.
 * @param mixed $value Value passed through the controller ViewBag.
 * @return void
 */
public function SetDefaultVariable(string $key, mixed $value): void
{
    if ($key === '') {
        return;
    }
    $this->defaultViewBag[$key] = $value;
}

Describe behavior as well as types. A useful cookie comment explains whether expiration is relative, whether the incoming cookie array changes, and what deletion requires. Array documentation can describe entry types, for example array<string, mixed> for view data.

Names used as named arguments are also part of the contract. Even a spelling correction can break a caller using that parameter name. The finished renderer therefore preserves the existing cutomLayout spelling.

Put the pieces together

The application entry point is now small because the library has taken over the repeated work. With the finished library, the Greeting model, the final HomeController::index() action, and the message view from step 10, demo/index.php can be:

<?php
require dirname(__DIR__) . '/vendor/autoload.php';

use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Demo\HomeController;
use Richie314\SimpleMvc\Routers\Router;

$router = new Router(applicationInstallationPath: __DIR__);
$router->AddController(HomeController::class, '/');
$router->Dispatch($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']);

After generating the development autoloader, start the local server:

composer install
php -S localhost:8000 -t demo demo/index.php

Visit http://localhost:8000/?name=Ada. The router selects index(), binds the name, and creates the controller. The action asks the model for a greeting and passes it to the view. The renderer places the view inside the layout and sends the response.

Try changing the name, omitting it, and requesting /missing. Then run the Docker checks before making the next change. Each feature now has a clear place: routing selects an action, the controller coordinates it, models hold application rules, and views present the result.

entry.title: Star Wars intro maker
entry.content:
For my web development exam, I presented a complete and accurate recreation of the Star Wars intros, built entirely with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript. I built the site so users could watch the original intros in both Italian and English, as well as create and edit custom ones through a form.

You can find my complete source code on GitHub.

Information:

A demo is available!

Go to https://starwars.ciucci.dev

In this step-by-step guide, I’ll walk you through how I recreated the intro.

1. Give the renderer a small, stable structure

We’ll start with a black page and these layers:

<body class="wait">
  
  <!-- Simple CSS only loader to show until media assets (audio) load -->
  <div id="loader">
    <div class="loader"></div>
  </div>
  
  <!-- Main 16:9 screen -->
  <main id="screen">
    <section class="intro">
      A long time ago in a galaxy far,<br />
      far away...
    </section>
    <section class="logo">
      <img src="logo.svg" alt="Star Wars">
    </section>

    <!-- Scrolling content -->
    <article id="board">
      <div id="content">
        <p id="episode">
          Episode X
        </p>
        <p id="title">
          The css awakens
        </p>
        <br />

        <p class="paragraph">
          Text here
        </p>
      </div>
    </article>
    <article id="credits" class="hidden">
      End credits to show the author
    </article>
  </main>
</body>

#screen is the visible cinema frame. .intro and .logo sit above the starfield. #board supplies the crawl’s tilted coordinate system; its child #content moves inside that system. By keeping those two responsibilities on separate elements, we can turn ordinary vertical text movement into movement into depth.

I suggest using three paragraphs to match the audio timing; we’ll see why later.

2. Make a responsive cinema frame

We’ll use a 16:9 frame that fits any viewport shape. Here is the CSS we’ll use to achieve this:

body {
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
  width: 100vw;
  height: 100vh;
  overflow: hidden;
  background-color: black;
  min-height: 80px;
}
#screen {
  overflow: hidden;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 !important;
  position: relative;
  width: 100vw;
  height: auto;
  font-size: 1.15vw;
  --percentageOfHeight: calc(100vw / 1600 * 9);
  margin: calc(50vh - 50 * var(--percentageOfHeight)) 0 auto 0;
}
@media screen and (min-aspect-ratio: 16 / 9) {
  #screen {
    width: auto;
    height: 100vh;
    margin: 0 auto;
    font-size: 2.3vh;
    --percentageOfHeight: 1vh;
  }
}

When the viewport is narrow or tall, the frame uses the full width. Its height is 100vw × 9/16. The custom property is one hundredth of that frame height: 100vw × 9/1600. Therefore 50vh - 50 × var(--percentageOfHeight) is half the leftover vertical space, centering the frame with black bars above and below.

On a wider viewport, height becomes the limiting dimension. A full-height 16:9 frame is horizontally centered by the auto margins, with black bars at its sides. position: relative makes the frame the containing block for its absolutely positioned layers. overflow: hidden clips the show to that frame.

3. Starfield background

We’ll create the starfield using a series of white <div> elements against a black background.

.star {
  position: absolute;
  width: 1.5px;
  height: 1.5px;
  background-color: rgba(249, 251, 242, 0.8);
  z-index: -1;
}
  .star.star-big {
    width: 4px;
    height: 4px;
    border: none;
    border-radius: 2px;
  }

Now let’s generate 100 of them and put them in random positions. Each star will have a 6% chance of being slightly larger.

for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) {
  const star = document.createElement('div');
  star.className = 'star';
  if (Math.random() > 0.94)
    star.classList.add('star-big');

  Object.assign(star.style, {
    top: `${Math.random() * 100}%`, 
    left: `${Math.random() * 100}%`
  });
  document.getElementById('screen').appendChild(star);
}

4. Blue opening sentence

We’ll place the opening blue text, A long time ago in a galaxy far, far away…, in the middle of #screen and use a @keyframes rule to fade it in and out.

.intro {
  position: absolute;
  top: 40%; 
  left: 15%;
  width: 70%; 
  height: 20%;
  z-index: 1;
  
  font-family: Century Gothic, CenturyGothic, AppleGothic, sans-serif;
  font-size: 2.6em;
  font-weight: 400;
  text-align: left;
  color: rgb(75, 213, 238);
  
  opacity: 0;
  animation: intro 5s ease-out 1s;
}
@keyframes intro {
  0%   { opacity: 0; }
  20%  { opacity: 1; }
  90%  { opacity: 1; }
  100% { opacity: 0; }
}

Together with the base opacity: 0 declaration, these keyframes keep the text hidden before and after the animation. Once we remove the loading class, it will start after a one-second delay and run for five seconds. We’ll raise the opacity to 1 to reveal the text, then lower it back to 0.

5. “STAR WARS” logo

I used an SVG image for the logo so the browser can rasterize its vector outlines at the size needed during scaling. A bitmap at insufficient resolution would look soft at the large initial size. We’ll use an ordinary <img> here: CSS transforms the whole image, rather than animating paths inside the SVG.

.logo {
  position: absolute;
  top: 2.5%;
  left: 2.5%;
  width: 95%;
  height: fit-content;

  z-index: 1;
  overflow: hidden;
  opacity: 0;
  user-select: none;

  animation: logo 13s linear 7s;
  transform-origin: center;
}
  .logo img { 
    width: 100%; 
    height: auto;
  }
@keyframes logo {
  0%   { transform: scale(1.25); opacity: 1; }
  10%  { transform: scale(1.1);  opacity: 1; }
  20%  { transform: scale(.85);  opacity: 1; }
  30%  { transform: scale(.7);   opacity: 1; }
  40%  { transform: scale(.6);   opacity: 1; }
  50%  { transform: scale(.5);   opacity: 1; }
  60%  { transform: scale(.42);  opacity: 1; }
  70%  { transform: scale(.34);  opacity: 1; }
  80%  { transform: scale(.26);  opacity: 1; }
  90%  { transform: scale(.18);  opacity: .8; }
  100% { transform: scale(.1);   opacity: 0; }
}

At seven seconds the logo appears already enlarged to 125% of its box. It shrinks around its center until 20 seconds into the scene.

Opacity stays at one through 80% of the animation (17.4 seconds), then fades toward zero. linear interpolates each segment uniformly, but unequal scale differences between stops mean the overall scale change is not one constant rate.

This is a 2D scale illusion, as the logo does not share the crawl’s perspective transform.

6. The perspective plane

Now let’s add the core geometry:

#board {
  color: #E2C64E;
  font-family: Century Gothic, CenturyGothic, AppleGothic, sans-serif;
  font-weight: bold;
  user-select: none;

  transform: perspective(calc(var(--percentageOfHeight) * 100))
             rotateX(35deg);
  transform-origin: 50% 100%;
  overflow: hidden;
  height: calc(350 * var(--percentageOfHeight));
  width: 95%;
  margin: auto 2.5% 0 2.5%;

  position: absolute;
  bottom: 0; 
  left: 0;
}

We’ll call the frame height H. The custom property is H/100, so the board is 3.5H tall, and the perspective distance is H. Its bottom edge is anchored to the frame bottom. Much of the untransformed board extends above the frame; the transform projects that tall rectangle into a narrowing plane.

transform-origin: 50% 100% places the pivot at the bottom center. rotateX(35deg) tilts the top away from the viewer while keeping that pivot in place. CSS transform composition matters: in perspective(H) rotateX(35deg), the rotation acts on points before the perspective projection. Swapping the functions changes the result.

We can use a simplified calculation to explain the narrowing. Let’s call a point’s distance upward from the bottom pivot d. Before projection, its coordinates relative to that pivot are approximately:

y = -d × cos(35°)
z = -d × sin(35°)
scale = H / (H - z)
      = H / (H + d × sin(35°))

At the pivot, d = 0, so the perspective scale is one. Farther upward, z becomes more negative and the denominator grows: the same line of text projects smaller. This is why parallel edges converge and distant lines become compressed. These equations describe the transform around the pivot; CSS layout then positions the transformed plane in the frame.

A smaller perspective distance exaggerates the convergence. A larger distance flattens it. Increasing the angle lays the board farther back. I suggest changing one parameter at a time because the angle, board height, and typography jointly determine how much text is visible.

7. Main text

We’ll use large text in the board’s local coordinates:

#content {
  position: absolute;
  top: 100%;
  width: 100%;
  color: inherit;
  animation: scroll 140s linear 18s;
}
.paragraph {
  color: inherit;
  font-size: 5.1em;
  word-break: keep-all;
  text-align: justify;
  user-select: none;
}
#episode, #title {
  color: inherit;
  text-align: center;
  font-size: 5.8em;
  overflow-x: visible;
  overflow-y: hidden;
  word-break: keep-all;
}
#title { 
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
@keyframes scroll {
  from { top: 100%; }
  to   { top: -200%; }
}

The animation starts at scene time 18 seconds, overlapping the last two seconds of the logo. Over 140 seconds, #content travels from one board-height below the board’s top to two board-heights above it. Percentage top values refer to the board’s height, not the text’s height or the viewport.

Since the board is 3.5H, the total travel is 3 × 3.5H = 10.5H. The local speed is 10.5H / 140s = 0.075H/s. It is linear in the tilted plane, but projected movement becomes slower as the text recedes. Perspective creates that apparent deceleration without any JavaScript motion loop.

The board clips its children, and the frame clips the whole scene. At 158 seconds the animation ends. With no forwards fill, top returns to its base 100%, below the visible board.

We’ll justify the paragraphs and center the episode number and title. The CSS relies on system font fallbacks and browser default paragraph margins and line height; these influence wrapping, spacing, and the eventual credits estimate.

Longer writing does not increase the 140-second scroll duration. It adds content below the start position, so sufficiently long text can remain unread when the animation ends.

8. Initial loader

We’ll add an initial loading gate so the CSS animations don’t start before the audio and stylesheets are available. We’ll give the body the wait class initially:

.hidden { 
  display: none !important;
}
#loader { 
  display: none;
}
  body.wait #loader {
    position: absolute;
    width: 100%; 
    height: 100%;
    top: 0; 
    left: 0;

    display: flex;
    justify-content: center;
    align-items: center;

    filter: none;
    z-index: 100;
  }
    body.wait *:not(#loader, .loader) {
      filter: blur(1.5px);
      animation-name: none !important;
      animation-delay: unset !important;
    }

This removes animation names while waiting; it does not pause animations halfway through. Removing .wait restores the declarations and starts their delay clocks together.

The loading spinner uses two perpendicular pairs of bars painted with linear gradients. A ::before pseudo-element repeats those bars rotated 45 degrees, yielding eight bars. A conic-gradient mask varies their opacity around the circle.

@keyframes Loader {
  from { transform: rotate(0turn); }
  to   { transform: rotate(1turn); }
}
.loader { 
  animation: Loader 1s steps(8) infinite;
}

steps(8) advances in eight jumps per second, rather than rotating smoothly.

In the head, we’ll load the JavaScript before the stylesheets so their onload handlers exist:

<script src="view.js" data-audio-url="intro.mp3"></script>
<link rel="stylesheet" href="view.css" onload="PageStyleLoaded()">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="animations.css" onload="PageAnimationsLoaded()">

The JavaScript captures document.currentScript.dataset.audioUrl during script execution. The application then injects the correct asset URL there.

var audioLoaded = false;
var pageStyleLoaded = false;
var pageAnimationsLoaded = false;

function CheckLoad() {
  if (document.readyState === 'loading' || !audioLoaded || !pageStyleLoaded || !pageAnimationsLoaded) 
      return;
  StartPage();
}
function AudioLoaded() { 
  audioLoaded = true; 
  CheckLoad();
}
function PageStyleLoaded() { 
  pageStyleLoaded = true; 
  CheckLoad();
}
function PageAnimationsLoaded() { 
  pageAnimationsLoaded = true; 
  CheckLoad();
}

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', CheckLoad);
audio.addEventListener('loadeddata', () => AudioLoaded());

The audio object is created in the next step, before these listeners are registered. We should keep in mind that the loadeddata event means media data has become available; it does not guarantee that the entire track has downloaded or that playback will never stall.

StartPage() records the scene epoch and removes .wait:

const Now = () => performance.now();
var start = 0;
function StartPage() {
  start = Now();
  document.body.classList.remove('wait');
  StartAudio();
}

performance.now() gives elapsed milliseconds from a monotonic clock, avoiding wall-clock adjustments. CSS becomes active on rendering updates, so this is a practical shared epoch, not a guarantee of sample-accurate synchronization.

9. Music and timing

Here are the timing values we’ll use:

Event Time after releasing .wait
Blue sentence starts / ends 1 s / 6 s
Audio file starts at offset zero 6.3 s
Logo starts / ends 7 s / 20 s
Crawl starts / ends 18 s / 158 s
Credits scheduling begins 105 s, then a content-based delay

The soundtrack starts 700 ms before the logo, not when the logo appears.

I used this timing in the renderer to match the soundtrack. All the delays depend on the audio file we use; the values in this article are specific to the file in my demo.

We’ll create the audio object and control when playback starts:

const AUDIO_START_DELAY = 6300;
function CreateAudio() {
  const audio = new Audio(audioSource);
  audio.autoplay = false;
  audio.muted = false;
  audio.preload = 'auto';
  return audio;
}
const audio = CreateAudio();

We’d like to start the audio once it has loaded, but browser autoplay policies may require the user to interact with the page first. We’ll use a click handler to retry playback and seek to the appropriate position so the audio matches the ongoing animations.

function StartAudio() {
  if (!audio.paused) 
    return;
  
  const deltaT = Now() - start - AUDIO_START_DELAY;
  if (deltaT < 0) {
    setTimeout(StartAudio, -deltaT);
    return;
  }
  if (deltaT >= audio.duration * 1000) 
    return;
  audio.currentTime = deltaT / 1000;
  audio.play().then(
    () => console.log('Audio started')
  ).catch(
    () => console.warn('Audio will start when the user clicks on the page')
  );
}
document.addEventListener('click', () => StartAudio());

We’ll handle three cases:

  1. Too early: a negative deltaT schedules another attempt at the cue. A timeout may run late, so the next call recomputes the offset.
  2. On time or late: seek the track to the position it should have reached, then attempt playback. currentTime uses seconds; performance.now() and the delay use milliseconds, hence the division by 1000.
  3. Past the end: leave the finished track silent, rather than restarting it.

For example, a click at scene time 12 seconds requests audio position 12 - 6.3 = 5.7 seconds. A click at 3 seconds schedules a future attempt; it does not start the music immediately. Because that later attempt is asynchronous, an early click may still fail to satisfy a browser’s autoplay policy. A click after the cue retries play() directly in the click handler.

We’re using a seek-on-start synchronization approach. While audio is already playing, the early return prevents correction.

10. Closing credits

We’ll wait 105 seconds before scheduling the closing credits, then add a delay based on the text length.

const CREDITS_SHOW_DELAY = 105 * 1000;
// Inside StartPage():
setTimeout(() => {
  const additional_delay = Math.sqrt(ContentLength() + 10) * 2100;
  if (!isNaN(additional_delay) && additional_delay > 0) {
    setTimeout(show_credits, additional_delay);
  } else {
    show_credits();
  }
}, CREDITS_SHOW_DELAY);

ContentLength() reads #content.getBoundingClientRect().height, temporarily appends a .paragraph containing A, measures its height, removes it, and rounds the ratio. It returns zero for NaN or negative estimates.

This is an approximate measure, not a count of rendered text lines. The content includes headings, margins, and spacing, and getBoundingClientRect() reflects transformed geometry. The temporary paragraph can also be at a different depth from the content it is meant to measure. I use the square-root formula as a heuristic; it is not derived from the scroll speed.

For a returned estimate of 30, the extra wait is sqrt(40) × 2.1 ≈ 13.28 seconds, putting the reveal at about 118.28 seconds. Even an estimate of zero adds sqrt(10) × 2.1 ≈ 6.64 seconds.

The reveal itself removes display: none, permits text selection, waits one more second, and starts a CSS opacity transition:

function show_credits() {
  credits.classList.remove('hidden');
  credits.style.userSelect = 'text';
  setTimeout(() => credits.style.opacity = 1, 1000);
}

#credits {
  position: absolute;
  z-index: 50;
  opacity: 0;
  transition: opacity 1.4s ease-in;
}

We’ll leave a one-second gap so the browser can render the credits in a transparent state before the opacity changes.

11. Keep the presentation unobtrusive

Finally, we’ll use JavaScript to suppress the context menu and hide the pointer after inactivity. We’ll hide the pointer with a .no-cursor class. Whenever the mouse moves, we’ll remove that class, clear the previous timeout, and schedule a new one to hide the pointer after two seconds. We’ll also set an initial timer to hide it after three seconds if the mouse never moves:

.no-cursor { 
  cursor: none;
}

entry.title: Sorting algorithms overview
entry.content:
• computer-science
  • algorithms
  • data-structures
  • cpp
  • visualization

I made these interactive sorting tools as a school project during my fourth year of high school. I wanted to turn the algorithms we were studying into something I could watch: values moving across an array, one comparison or exchange at a time.

In this article, I’ll use those tools to explain eight sorting algorithms, from bubble sort to merge sort. We’ll look at the idea behind each one, follow a small example, and connect what happens on screen to its computational cost.

How to use the simulations

Each bar represents an array element: taller bars have larger values. The goal is to arrange them in ascending order, from the shortest bar on the left to the tallest on the right. Small arrays also display their values. Every canvas has a gray-white background, with blue array bars, muted red active values, orange comparisons, and green settled positions. The legend below each canvas identifies these colors.

I suggest starting with 16 or 32 elements and a delay of 100 milliseconds. Click Shuffle to prepare an array, then Sort to run the animation. Use Pause and Resume to inspect a step or continue from where you stopped. Clicking Shuffle during a run stops it and resets its counter. The Array size field controls how many values the next shuffle generates; Step delay (ms) controls the animation delay in milliseconds. For a fresh comparison, choose the array size and click Shuffle before starting.

The counters describe different kinds of work. Most demos count swaps; Shell sort counts array writes, including shifts and reinsertion; merge sort counts writes back into the array. These are useful observations within one algorithm, but they are not interchangeable measures of runtime. The animations also wait at different points, so their elapsed times are not benchmarks.

What complexity tells us

We’ll call the number of elements \(n\). Time complexity describes how an algorithm’s work grows as \(n\) increases, assuming comparisons, assignments, and swaps of individual values take constant time. Auxiliary space counts additional working memory, including recursive calls, but excludes the input array.

\(O(f(n))\) gives an asymptotic upper bound; \(\Theta(f(n))\) gives a tight growth bound. A quadratic algorithm does roughly four times as much work when we double a large input. An \(n\log n\) algorithm grows more slowly: for example, \(n^2=1{,}048{,}576\) and \(n\log_2 n=10{,}240\) when \(n=1024\). These expressions illustrate growth, rather than exact operation counts.

The best case is the most favorable arrangement, the worst case is the least favorable, and the average case below assumes a uniformly random permutation of distinct values. A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal keys. For example, if two student records have the same grade, a stable sort by grade keeps them in their original order.

The table describes the C++ examples below. Every sorting function takes a std::vector<T>& and sorts the half-open range [start, end), including start and excluding end. For example, with std::vector<int> values = {4, 2, 3, 1};, call BubbleSort(values, 0, values.size()) to sort the entire vector in place. Each example includes its required standard headers: <vector>, <cstddef> for std::size_t, and <utility> for std::swap where needed. They assume start <= end <= arr.size() and values with consistent < and > comparisons. Passing the vector by reference lets us modify it without copying the entire input; merge sort allocates a separate temporary vector when merging.

Implementation choices matter. Adding early stopping changes bubble sort’s best case; changing Shell sort’s gaps changes its bounds. Princeton’s sorting summary is a useful reference for the standard algorithms, while these sorting lecture notes discuss the quadratic worst case of Shell’s original gap sequence.

Bubble sort

We’ll start with adjacent pairs. If the left value is larger, we swap the pair. After one left-to-right pass, the largest value in the active range has reached its final position at the right edge. Each new pass can therefore stop one element earlier.

For [4, 2, 3, 1], the first pass produces [2, 3, 1, 4]. The 4 is settled, even though the rest of the array still needs work. In the animation, watch the sorted suffix grow from right to left.

This fixed-pass version performs the same number of comparisons for every arrangement:

\[C(n)=(n-1)+(n-2)+\cdots+1=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.\]

Its time is therefore \(\Theta(n^2)\), even on sorted input, although sorted input requires no swaps. We could add a flag to stop after a swap-free pass and obtain a \(\Theta(n)\) best case. The version here deliberately keeps the fixed passes. It uses constant auxiliary space and is stable because equal neighbors are never exchanged.

template <typename T>
void BubbleSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    for (std::size_t limit = end; limit > start; --limit) {
        for (std::size_t j = start; j + 1 < limit; ++j) {
            if (arr[j] > arr[j + 1])
                std::swap(arr[j], arr[j + 1]);
        }
    }
}

Cocktail shaker sort

Cocktail shaker sort takes bubble sort in both directions. We’ll move the largest remaining value to the right with a forward pass, then move the smallest remaining value to the left with a backward pass. After that round, both boundaries can move inward.

With [2, 3, 4, 1], an ordinary forward bubble pass moves the 1 left by only one position. A backward pass can carry it all the way to the beginning. I suggest watching how small values travel left in this demo, rather than only following large values to the right.

The fixed-pass implementation below still scans a quadratic number of adjacent pairs, so its best, average, and worst times are all \(\Theta(n^2)\). Alternating direction changes the movement pattern without changing that growth rate. As with bubble sort, a swap-free-pass check can make an optimized version linear on sorted input. Strict adjacent comparisons keep this version stable, and its auxiliary space is \(\Theta(1)\).

void ShakerSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    if (end - start < 2) return;
    std::size_t left = start, right = end - 1;
    while (left < right) {
        for (std::size_t i = left; i < right; ++i)
            if (arr[i] > arr[i + 1])
                std::swap(arr[i], arr[i + 1]);
        --right;
        for (std::size_t i = right; i > left; --i)
            if (arr[i] < arr[i - 1])
                std::swap(arr[i], arr[i - 1]);
        ++left;
    }
}

Insertion sort

Here we’ll maintain a sorted prefix. We take the next value and move it left until it reaches the correct position inside that prefix. This is similar to inserting a new card into an already ordered hand.

For [2, 4, 5, 3], the prefix [2, 4, 5] is sorted. We exchange 3 with 5, then with 4, producing [2, 3, 4, 5]. The animation makes this repeated movement through the prefix visible.

An inversion is a pair of indices \(i<j\) with \(a_i>a_j\). Every adjacent swap in insertion sort removes exactly one inversion. If the input has \(I\) inversions, its running time is \(\Theta(n+I)\). Sorted input has none, giving a \(\Theta(n)\) best case. Reverse-sorted distinct input has the maximum:

\[I_{\max}=\binom{n}{2}=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}.\]

A uniformly random permutation has \(n(n-1)/4\) inversions on average, so both average and worst time are \(\Theta(n^2)\). This also explains why insertion sort works well on nearly sorted data. We need constant extra space, and equal values retain their order.

    if (end - start < 2) return;
    for (std::size_t i = start + 1; i < end; ++i) {
        std::size_t j = i;
        while (j > start && arr[j] < arr[j - 1]) {
            std::swap(arr[j], arr[j - 1]);
            --j;
        }
    }
}

Selection sort

Instead of exchanging every out-of-order pair, we’ll search the entire unsorted suffix for its minimum and swap that minimum into the next position. The sorted prefix grows by one value per pass.

For [4, 2, 3, 1], the first search finds 1 and exchanges it with 4, giving [1, 2, 3, 4]. Even though this particular array is now sorted, the remaining searches still run: selection sort does not use existing order to skip them.

The number of comparisons is again \(n(n-1)/2\), giving \(\Theta(n^2)\) time in all three cases. The example skips self-swaps and makes at most \(n-1\) actual swaps, using \(\Theta(1)\) auxiliary space. That separation between many comparisons and relatively few writes is its main distinction here.

Selection sort is not stable. Label equal values to see why: sorting [2A, 2B, 1] begins by exchanging 2A with 1, leaving [1, 2B, 2A]. The two equal keys have changed relative order.

template <typename T>
void SelectionSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    for (std::size_t i = start; i < end; ++i) {
        std::size_t minimum = i;
        for (std::size_t j = i + 1; j < end; ++j)
            if (arr[j] < arr[minimum]) minimum = j;
        if (minimum != i) std::swap(arr[i], arr[minimum]);
    }
}

Odd-even sort

Odd–even sort, also called brick sort, alternates between two sets of adjacent pairs. Using zero-based indices, one phase checks (0, 1), (2, 3), …; the other checks (1, 2), (3, 4), …. Each pair is exchanged if it is out of order.

We’ll repeat both phases until an entire two-phase cycle makes no swaps. A single quiet phase is insufficient: [1, 3, 2, 4] needs no exchanges in the even-indexed pairs, but its middle pair is still reversed. The C++ example below explicitly checks the full cycle.

Each cycle costs \(\Theta(n)\); difficult inputs need a linear number of cycles, producing \(\Theta(n^2)\) average and worst time. Sorted input finishes after one full cycle, so the best case is \(\Theta(n)\). Strict adjacent swaps make it stable, and it needs \(\Theta(1)\) extra space.

Pairs within one phase do not overlap, which makes the algorithm interesting for parallel execution. This browser simulation runs sequentially; the bounds here describe sequential work.

template <typename T>
void OddEvenSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    if (end - start < 2) return;
    bool changed;
    do {
        changed = false;
        for (std::size_t phase = 0; phase < 2; ++phase) {
            for (std::size_t i = start + phase; i + 1 < end; i += 2) {
                if (arr[i] > arr[i + 1]) {
                    std::swap(arr[i], arr[i + 1]);
                    changed = true;
                }
            }
        }
    } while (changed);
}

Shell sort

Shell sort extends insertion sort by comparing values several positions apart. We’ll first insertion-sort subsequences separated by a large gap, then reduce the gap and repeat. The final gap of one is an ordinary insertion-sort pass, but earlier passes have already moved values closer to their destinations.

The gap sequence here is \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\lfloor n/4\rfloor,\ldots,1\). With eight elements, the gaps are 4, 2, 1. At gap four, indices (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 6), and (3, 7) form separate subsequences. Watch how values can move across the array much earlier than in adjacent-swap insertion sort.

On sorted input, each gap pass still visits roughly \(n\) values, and there are \(\Theta(\log n)\) passes, giving \(\Theta(n\log n)\) best time. This halving sequence has a \(\Theta(n^2)\) worst case. I use a conservative \(O(n^2)\) upper bound for its average time rather than assigning Shell sort a universal average-case exponent: the gap sequence is part of the algorithm’s analysis.

The implementation uses \(\Theta(1)\) auxiliary space. It is not stable because long-distance movements can carry equal keys past one another. Its counter includes reinserting the saved value as well as shifting preceding values, so it measures array writes rather than swaps.

#include <cstddef>

template <typename T>
void ShellSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    for (std::size_t gap = (end - start) / 2; gap > 0; gap /= 2) {
        for (std::size_t i = start + gap; i < end; ++i) {
            T value = arr[i];
            std::size_t j = i;
            while (j - start >= gap && arr[j - gap] > value) {
                arr[j] = arr[j - gap];
                j -= gap;
            }
            arr[j] = value;
        }
    }
}

Quicksort

Quicksort partitions an array around a pivot, then recursively sorts the two sides. In this version, we’ll choose the last value as the pivot, collect values less than or equal to it on the left, and finally place the pivot between the partitions. The pivot is then in its final sorted position.

For [4, 1, 3, 2], the pivot is 2. Partitioning produces [1, 2, 3, 4], with 2 settled. In general, the two sides still need recursive sorting; partitioning does not sort them internally.

When partitions are balanced, each recursion level does \(\Theta(n)\) work across its subarrays, and there are \(\Theta(\log n)\) levels:

\[T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n\log n).\]

The average time for uniformly random distinct input is also \(\Theta(n\log n)\). However, choosing the last element gives extremely uneven partitions on already sorted, reverse-sorted, or all-equal input:

\[T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)=\Theta(n^2).\]

I suggest comparing the balanced and unbalanced recurrences: quicksort’s performance depends on the shape of its recursion tree. Randomizing pivot selection helps avoid predictable bad inputs, while three-way partitioning handles repeated keys more effectively.

Partitioning uses constant working space, but recursive calls need \(\Theta(\log n)\) space for balanced partitions and \(\Theta(n)\) in the worst case. This implementation is not stable. Its half-open ranges also avoid subtracting one from a zero-valued unsigned pivot index.

#include <cstddef>

template <typename T>
std::size_t Partition(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    T pivot = arr[end - 1];
    std::size_t boundary = start;
    for (std::size_t j = start; j < end - 1; ++j) {
        if (!(pivot < arr[j])) { // arr[j] <= pivot
            std::swap(arr[boundary], arr[j]);
            ++boundary;
        }
    }
    std::swap(arr[boundary], arr[end - 1]);
    return boundary;
}

template <typename T>
void QuickSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    if (end - start < 2) return;
    std::size_t pivot = Partition(arr, start, end);
    QuickSort(arr, start, pivot);
    QuickSort(arr, pivot + 1, end);
}

Merge sort

Merge sort also divides the problem, but its split is always near the middle. We’ll recursively sort the two halves, then merge them by repeatedly taking the smaller of their first unconsumed values. A one-element range is already sorted.

For [4, 1, 3, 2], we split into [4, 1] and [3, 2], sort those into [1, 4] and [2, 3], then merge them into [1, 2, 3, 4].

Merging two halves with a total of \(n\) elements takes \(\Theta(n)\) work. Balanced splitting gives the same recurrence as balanced quicksort:

\[T(n)=T(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)+T(\lceil n/2\rceil)+\Theta(n) =\Theta(n\log n).\]

The difference is the guarantee: these splits stay balanced for every input. This version always merges, so best, average, and worst time are all \(\Theta(n\log n)\). We could optimize it by checking whether the halves already meet in order, but that check is not included here.

The temporary buffer requires \(\Theta(n)\) auxiliary space at peak; the \(\Theta(\log n)\) recursion stack does not change that overall bound. We take from the left half when keys are equal, preserving stability. I use a std::vector for the temporary values so their lifetimes are managed correctly in C++. In the demo, the counter tracks writes back into the main array, not exchanges between two positions.

#include <cstddef>
#include <vector>

template <typename T>
void Merge(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t middle, std::size_t end) {
    std::vector<T> buffer(arr.begin() + start, arr.begin() + end);
    const std::size_t leftEnd = middle - start;
    std::size_t i = 0, j = leftEnd, k = start;
    while (i < leftEnd && j < buffer.size()) {
        // Choose the left value on equal keys to preserve stability.
        if (!(buffer[j] < buffer[i])) arr[k++] = buffer[i++];
        else arr[k++] = buffer[j++];
    }
    while (i < leftEnd) arr[k++] = buffer[i++];
    while (j < buffer.size()) arr[k++] = buffer[j++];
}

template <typename T>
void MergeSort(std::vector<T>& arr, std::size_t start, std::size_t end) {
    if (end - start < 2) return;
    std::size_t middle = start + (end - start) / 2;
    MergeSort(arr, start, middle);
    MergeSort(arr, middle, end);
    Merge(arr, start, middle, end);
}

What I suggest comparing

Start with bubble sort and selection sort on arrays of the same size. Their comparison counts grow quadratically, but selection sort makes far fewer swaps. Next, compare insertion sort with Shell sort and watch the difference between adjacent movement and movement across a gap. Finally, run quicksort and merge sort on larger arrays to see partitioning and merging produce two different visual patterns.

The shuffle controls generate distinct values rather than custom inputs, so the demos do not directly expose every best or worst case. To observe sorted input, finish a run and click Sort again without shuffling. To explore those cases, I suggest running the C++ examples on sorted, reverse-sorted, and duplicate-heavy arrays. To investigate stability, use records with a key and an identity, and compare only the key.

All eight methods here are comparison sorts. A comparison can distinguish at most two outcomes for distinct keys, and a correct sort must distinguish among \(n!\) possible input orders. A decision tree therefore needs worst-case height at least

\[\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil=\Omega(n\log n).\]

That lower bound explains why merge sort’s worst-case growth is optimal in this model. It does not apply to every possible sorting method: algorithms such as counting sort use extra assumptions about the keys. Princeton’s introduction to sorting provides a path into these broader topics.

For me, the value of this school project is the connection between the code and its behavior. We can watch where values move, identify the invariant each pass maintains, and then explain why the amount of work grows the way it does.
